questions.question: The dependency loses support in ten weeks. Migration is estimated at three to five weeks. When does the decision itself expire?
options: Around week five, because after that the pessimistic five-week path no longer fits inside the window
At week ten, when support actually ends
Around week seven, using the midpoint of the three-to-five week estimate
There is no expiry, because nothing breaks immediately at end-of-support
questions.explanation: A time-boxed decision expires before its deadline by the duration of the work it authorises, and you size that duration from the pessimistic end, not the average. Option C is the tempting one — using the midpoint looks balanced, but it quietly bets on the optimistic half of an estimate that engineering already called wide.

questions.question: Four engineers disagree about migration timing. The PM says: "You four know the code, so decide it among yourselves and tell me." What is wrong?
options: Nothing — specialist authority should decide questions inside its expertise
The PM should decide it, because roadmap timing is a product responsibility
The engineers hold specialist authority but not the roadmap consequence, so a decider with that consequence still has to sign
The disagreement should be escalated to the engineering lead's manager
questions.explanation: Specialist authority and decider are different roles. The engineers can settle what is technically possible; none of them carries the cost of the cycle being spent this way. Option A is the answer a PM gives after learning to respect expertise — it sounds humble, but it leaves a consequential call with no accountable signer.

questions.question: A PM escalates a contentious decision to the head of product, who makes the call. It goes badly. What is the PM's position?
options: The consequence transferred with the decision, so accountability now sits with the head of product
The PM still owns the outcome in their area; escalation added a name to the record, not a transfer of consequence
The escalation was the error, since consequential decisions should never move upward
Accountability is shared equally between the two, since both took part
questions.explanation: Architecture is not a permission system. Escalate to get a decision that genuinely is not yours, not to distribute blame. Option D is the comfortable answer that most teams settle for, and it produces a record in which nobody can be asked what they learned.

questions.question: A decision has been discussed in three long meetings with wide participation and still has no answer. The PM proposes adding a formal review stage. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the right specialists have been in the room
Whether the participants have enough evidence to reach a conclusion
Whether the review would fit before the deadline
Whether the decision is stated as a choice with live alternatives, or is still a topic
questions.explanation: Process cannot rescue a badly framed decision. Adding rigor to "what should we do about the dependency" produces a more expensive version of the same confusion. Option B is the trained answer — but a group given a real choice and a date will usually decide on the evidence they already hold.

questions.question: Which pair of decisions is being routed correctly?
options: Empty-state copy variant: decided by the PM in a day, reviewed from its outcome. Storage-layer change: decided with the engineering lead as specialist authority, reviewed before commitment
Empty-state copy variant: taken to the weekly forum for team alignment. Storage-layer change: decided by the two engineers closest to it in a direct message
Both taken to the weekly forum, so that decisions stay comparable and the team stays informed
Both decided by the PM, since the PM owns the roadmap consequence in each case
questions.explanation: Rigor and review depth should follow consequence and reversibility: reversible work is reviewed from its outcome, one-way work before commitment. Option C is the tempting answer because consistency reads as discipline — but a uniform forum over-spends process on the cheap decision and adds no real scrutiny to the expensive one.
